paras: The lynching of Joseph Prescott was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a band of white "regulators" in southeastern Pike County, Mississippi, near Dillon's Bridge, after midnight on the night of Sunday, April 8, 1888. The same band reportedly beat Frank Warner, a Black boy of about fifteen, into accusing Prescott and the brothers Hardy and Ben Kaigler of trying to rob a store, then whipped the Kaiglers. A coroner's jury charged twenty-four white men and seventeen were arrested, while residents near the scene publicly disputed the Magnolia Gazette's account.

According to the Magnolia Gazette, several men in the southeastern part of the county "disliked certain of their colored neighbors," Hardy Kaigler, Ben Kaigler and Joseph Prescott, and had for some time sought information that would justify "regulating" them. A correspondent of the Summit Sentinel later wrote that such squads had organized about two years earlier and that their motive was "to drive from our county the colored population."

The Gazette reported that on Friday night the men seized Warner and beat him to make him inform against the three, without success. On Sunday night they caught him again and, with a rope around his neck, told him he would be hanged unless he answered yes, and he then said the men had tried to break into a store at Dillon's Bridge. Taking Warner along, the band put the two Kaiglers under guard, then went past midnight to Prescott's house on Richard Fortimberry's plantation and called him out.

Prescott broke loose and ran, and of several shots fired by the crowd one struck him just above the right hip; he died of the wound on Monday. The men then whipped the Kaiglers "in a most brutal manner," leaving one for dead by the roadside, though both survived.

The Gazette reported that a coroner's jury sat on Tuesday over Prescott's body and returned a verdict charging twenty-four white men with the crime. Sheriff A. A. Boyd and a posse of twelve rode all night and arrested seventeen of those named, who were brought before Justice of the Peace I. M. Ellzey, with a preliminary trial set for Thursday. The Gazette later wrote that witnesses had been examined before the committing court and that Warner swore he had been whipped on the Friday night before the killing.
A young man of fourteen or fifteen, described as not of sound mind, was also arrested on the murder charge, and no report of the hearing's outcome, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Magnolia Gazette broke the story on April 14 under the headline "Bull-Dozing. Three Negroes Whipped and One Killed," calling Warner "the poor boy" and the attackers "assassins." A Magnolia telegram of April 17 in the Omaha Daily Bee, headed "Lawless Regulators," followed the Gazette's wording closely and called the men "self-constituted regulators." A shorter Chicago dispatch ran in the Ohio Democrat of Logan, Ohio, on April 28 as "Regulators at Work in Mississippi"; it omitted Prescott's death.

At home the story became a local controversy, and on May 5 the Gazette printed the residents' denial beside an editorial standing by its account. On May 12 it reprinted "A Dark Corner," an "Anti-Bulldozer" letter from the Summit Sentinel calling the denial "an article written by one of the Bull-leezers" and the movement "a species of anarchy."

The residents' statement, signed by Josiah Brumfield and others, said the accused had always been on the best of terms with the Kaiglers and Prescott and denied any plan to "regulate" them. It denied that Warner had been beaten or roped, saying that on Monday, April 9, two or three men took him from a field and carried him on horseback to the inquest. The signers called the inquest secret, mentioned "some little display of fire-arms" there, and said Prescott had named six attackers before his death, four living in Louisiana, none of them arrested.

They also claimed the coroner's jury had not charged the twenty-four white men. The Gazette answered that witnesses before the committing court had confirmed its account, and the Summit Sentinel correspondent wrote that the sworn evidence placed the guilt "closer to our doors" than Louisiana.

reader.title: Lynching of Joseph Prescott
bases: A band of white men seized Black neighbors at night under an accusation of attempted store-breaking, shot Joseph Prescott dead as he fled, and whipped two others (A1, A2).

Prescott was shot dead by 'the crowd' of self-appointed 'regulators' acting without authority, after a forced accusation that he had tried to break into a store; the coroner's jury charged twenty-four white men, and even the defense statement says six men caused his death (A1, A2, A5).

The Gazette's report (A1) and the Magnolia telegram (A2, likely drawn from the same local source) are supported on the killing by both the residents' statement, which accepts that Prescott was killed by a group and named six men, and the Anti-Bulldozer letter (A5, A7); the residents dispute the Warner beatings and who was responsible (A4).

accounts.label: Magnolia Gazette (local editor)
accounts.gist: Neighbors who disliked the three Black men forced an accusation from Warner by beating and roping him, then seized the Kaiglers, shot Prescott as he fled, and whipped the Kaiglers; the coroner's jury charged twenty-four white men.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Magnolia and Chicago dispatches described a band of regulators flogging Black men; the fuller version reports Prescott's fatal shooting, the shorter omits it.

accounts.label: Residents' statement (defense side)
accounts.gist: The accused were on good terms with the victims and Warner was not beaten or roped; the inquest was secret with firearms shown; Prescott named six men, four from Louisiana, who were never arrested.

accounts.label: Anti-Bulldozer correspondent
accounts.gist: The residents' statement was written by one of the bulldozers; sworn evidence pointed to local men in an organization formed to drive out the Black population.

Omaha Bee 'Lawless Regulators' and Ohio Democrat 'Regulators at Work in Mississippi' carried short dispatches.
Residents' statement defended the accused and attacked the inquest and the arrests.
'A Dark Corner' called bulldozing 'a species of anarchy' to be suppressed.
